text:
For several months, Daniel dreamed about an apartment he had never lived in.

It had two rooms, a narrow kitchen, and a bathroom with a medicine cabinet whose mirror had darkened at the edges. Afternoon light lay across the floorboards. There was no furniture. The radiator ticked, though it was summer. Daniel knew, as one knows things in dreams, that the apartment belonged to him and Rachel, his first wife, and that they had forgotten to move in.

Rachel was usually there, wearing the blue wool coat she’d owned in the last year of their marriage. Sometimes she stood at the kitchen window; once, she brushed her teeth in the bathroom. Daniel woke convinced he had left something in the medicine cabinet.

He told himself the dream was ordinary. He and Rachel had been married nine years; of course his mind kept a few rooms. But the apartment seemed almost prosecutorial in its detail. He could see cracks in the enamel sink and knew the front door stuck near the bottom.

At breakfast, Isabel asked if he’d slept badly.

“I was back in that apartment,” he said.

“Your dream apartment?”

“Yes.”

“Was I there?”

“No.”

“Good,” she said. “I wouldn’t want to intrude on the proceedings.”

Isabel made jokes when she was uncertain. Daniel knew not to mistake that for indifference.

“What happens in it?” she asked.

“Nothing. Rachel’s there. I’m there. We don’t seem to be waiting for anything.”

“You’re waiting to move in,” Isabel said. “Or waiting to move out.”

He looked at her. “That’s good.”

“I charge by the hour.”

They had been together four years, long enough to develop their own cautions. Daniel didn’t ask her to reassure him that dreams were meaningless. She didn’t demand proof that the past was over. Still, some mornings they seemed to be discussing a third person, someone who had lived inside Daniel longer than either of them had known each other.

The dream returned the next week. Rachel stood in the empty bedroom, studying a line of sunlight on the floor.

“Do you know where we are?” Daniel asked.

She looked at him. “You always want to know where you are.”

Then she opened the closet, and he woke before he could see inside.

That evening, he told Isabel while she cut chard at the counter.

“Do you think the apartment is real?” she asked.

“Not the way the dream makes it seem.”

“But real in some other way?”

“I don’t know.”

Rachel and Daniel had once looked at apartments together, before they married. They’d seen a railroad flat above a locksmith and a kitchen so small Rachel said it seemed designed for one person who disliked cooking. Eventually, they bought a house instead.

“I don’t remember an apartment we didn’t live in,” Daniel said.

“Maybe you’re not supposed to,” Isabel replied.

That night, they sorted photographs from a box Daniel had brought down from the hall closet. One showed Rachel in a green dress beside him at a picnic table. They looked young, in the way of people who haven’t yet been disappointed by a future they’ve planned.

“I think about Rachel sometimes,” he said.

“I know.”

“Not because I want to go back.”

“I know that, too.”

“What do you miss?” she asked.

“Maybe being that young.”

“That’s convenient.”

“It’s true.”

“Do you miss her?”

Daniel looked at the photograph. “Sometimes I miss knowing what she would say.”

Isabel nodded. She wasn’t jealous, though that didn’t mean she was untouched. She had once told him the hardest part of being with someone was pretending not to notice what mattered to them.

The apartment kept returning. In one dream, water ran behind a wall. In another, Rachel sat beside a cardboard box marked BOOKS, though Daniel had never owned such a box with her. He began to think the dream was less a memory than a machine for making one, arranging pieces into a room where nobody had to explain why they were there.

In October, Isabel asked him to find a small screwdriver. Daniel searched a box of household odds and ends in the hall closet. At the bottom lay a ring of keys attached to a green plastic tag, faded almost white.

He knew the keys before he understood why. One had a long, narrow shaft; another was small and brass, its teeth worn. He held them in his palm. The metal was cold.

“Did you find the screwdriver?” Isabel asked.

“No.”

“Promising.”

Daniel turned the tag over. A number, written in Rachel’s handwriting, had blurred with time. He could make out a 4 and perhaps a 1.

Then memory arrived—not as a scene, but as rain on the back of his neck, a paper bag in his hand, and Rachel laughing because he was trying the wrong door.

They had looked at the apartment above the locksmith. It was the last place they saw before choosing the house. The landlord had lent them keys for a weekend so they could measure the rooms. They spent an afternoon there without furniture, eating takeout noodles on the floor and discussing what to do with the small second room. Rachel wanted a studio. Daniel wanted a desk and a door he could close. They were both embarrassed by how quickly the apartment became a picture of their future.

In the end, they chose the house. The apartment was too small, the building noisy, the landlord difficult. All true, none of it explaining why they’d kept the keys.

The memory widened. After returning them, they rented a canoe at a reservoir. Rachel had never canoed; Daniel had, as a boy, and steered with the confidence of someone corrected once by a man in a hat.

“You’re aiming for the reeds,” Rachel said.

“I’m not.”

“We’re going to hit them.”

They hit them. The canoe slid through the stems, and Rachel laughed so hard she had to put down her paddle. They spent the next hour going in circles. At the end, she sat in the bow with her shoes off and said, “I like being bad at something with you.”

Daniel remembered it with a clarity that shamed him. He had let the marriage be represented by its ending.

Isabel came to stand beside him. “What did you find?”

“Keys to an apartment Rachel and I looked at.”

“The dream apartment?”

“I think so.”

“The one above the locksmith?” she asked. “You told me about it once.”

“Did I?”

“You said the kitchen was too small.”

He laughed. “That sounds like me.”

She touched a key. “Do you want to keep them?”

“I thought I’d thrown them away.”

“Maybe they’re the keys’ dream.”

The number on the tag was too faded to be useful. The apartment had likely been renovated, the lock changed, the building sold. The keys weren’t evidence, just remnants of a decision, kept because nobody had noticed them.

That night, Daniel dreamed of the apartment, but Rachel wasn’t there. The rooms were empty. From the kitchen came the familiar tapping of the radiator. He opened the closet. Inside lay a wooden paddle, its handle worn smooth.

He woke before dawn and lay beside Isabel, listening to her breathe. In the morning, he told her about the paddle.

“A canoe paddle?” she said.

“I think so.”

“Your dream has become recreational.”

She paused. “There’s a place that rents canoes on the river in spring. I’ve never gone.”

In April, they rented one from a man in a shed who gave them life jackets and an unnecessary account of the weather. Isabel climbed into the bow. Daniel steadied the canoe while she settled herself.

“Do you know what you’re doing?” she asked.

“No.”

“Good. Neither do I.”

He pushed off. The canoe immediately turned toward the bank.

“Is this intentional?” Isabel asked.

“It’s a technique.”

“What’s it called?”

“Negotiating with the river.”

She laughed. Daniel corrected their course. They moved slowly downstream, passing a footbridge and a half-submerged shopping cart. Isabel paddled too hard on one side, swinging them toward a stand of reeds.

“You’re aiming for those,” Daniel said.

“I’m not.”

“We’re going to hit them.”

“We’re not.”

They hit them, gently. The canoe trembled among the stems. Isabel set down her paddle and laughed, one hand braced on the gunwale. Daniel laughed too. The day wasn’t the one he remembered with Rachel. It had only the water, the reeds, and the small indignity of being unable to steer. That was enough to let the memory be present without making it a rival.

When they returned the canoe, Isabel’s trouser cuffs were wet. She walked beside him toward the car, carrying her shoes.

“Do you think you’ll dream about the apartment again?” she asked.

“Probably.”

“Would you tell me?”

“Yes.”

“Even if I’m not in it?”

“Especially then.”

She nodded, as if this were a reasonable arrangement.

At home, Daniel put the old keys in a bowl on the counter. He didn’t know why he kept them. The apartment appeared once more in his sleep. A strip of evening light crossed the floor, and the radiator ticked. The rooms were still bare. He stood in the kitchen, aware of someone in the next room—not Rachel, not Isabel, but the person he had been when he thought every door led somewhere he could choose.

In the morning, Isabel sat at the table, reading the news on her phone.

“Anything happen?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“Good.”

He kissed the top of her head and put on the kettle. The keys lay in their bowl, old and useless. Outside, the day was pale and wet. The river, he thought, would be high.

Then he asked Isabel if she wanted to go back next weekend. She looked up, smiling, as if he had offered her something simple and real.
